title: Comfort is the centre of the conference
body: My reading, built on the counts below. The passage cited most across the conference is Mosiah 18:8–11, the baptismal covenant to "mourn with those that mourn", in six talks; second is Alma 7:11–12, the Savior who knows how to succor His people, in five. No session was built around either. Beside them run the conference's grief stories: Sister Runia's son, Elder Sikahema's grandparents burying an infant on the voyage, a missionary's father killed a week before she came home, Elder Eyring's friend who could only say "I can't fix this," President Eyring's widowed father thanking every nurse. Read together, the doctrine the conference came back to most is that the Savior carries grief with us, and asks us to carry it with each other.

title: Being seen
body: My reading. Four talks cite the Good Samaritan and three the pool of Bethesda, both stories of someone others walked past. Sister Chibota builds her talk on sawubona, "I see you". Elder Sinclair's woman at the well "walked to the well that day as a pariah". Elder Fale, Sister Chibota and Elder Stevenson return to being a child of God. President Farnes's story is a leader stopping him to ask, "Brother, tell me how you are really doing." And President Uchtdorf turns it round: the sacrament is "the only ordinance we receive during which we are not addressed by name". Under the announced themes, much of this conference is about noticing people.

title: The advice: turn to Christ, then to the person in front of you
body: My reading of the 184 invitations. About 63 of them, in 19 talks, ask for something done for another person, more than any other kind. Most are about how we see and treat the people near us: "Learn the name of someone who may feel unseen" (Sister Chibota); "minister to the person in front of us" (President Farnes); make sure "no one is ever sitting, standing, or walking alone" (Elder Fale); be "quick to help and slow to judge" (Elder Sinclair); be "a little more patient, a little kinder, more forgiving, more helpful, more neighborly" (President Uchtdorf); use the language of peacemakers (Elder Kyungu). President Eyring thanks those who pray "to know who the Lord would have you help for Him". The rest are about sharing and teaching the gospel, led by Bishop Douglas's seven invitations on missions and Brother Reid's on teaching. Around them sits the most widespread ask, to turn to Christ and trust Him (Elder Dube: "please come unto Christ"; Elder Kearon: "keep turning toward the Saviour"). And the means are small and daily: scriptures "every day" (Elder Cook); "Protect your sleep; go to bed early" (Sister Muñoz Spannaus). The counts come from tagging the invitation highlights by keyword and checking the tags by hand, so they are approximate.

title: The promise: strength for the load, and a love that cannot be lost
body:
My reading of the 196 promises. Listen to what the speakers promise, and to what they carefully do not. Hardly anyone promises that the trial will end. Elder Chigbundu: "The burden we carry may not always be removed, but our backs will be built to carry the load placed upon them." Elder Dunn: "Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not." Elder Eyring promises comfort for "times when we can't fix things on our own." Elder Hathaway: "In His time and way, Jesus Christ will deliver you." President Eyring's mother told him, "Life is a test", and the promise he holds out is the hymn's: "As thy days may demand, … so thy succor shall be."
The most common promise, in about two-thirds of the talks, is strength: help, lift, power to stand. Elder Kearon promises that "when we sink, our gentle Saviour is there to lift us up as we turn to Him", and adds, "There is no limit to how high you can climb with Him." Then come peace, comfort and joy, and the Holy Ghost as a constant companion.
Underneath them all, sixteen promises in eight talks say the same quiet thing: what God gives cannot be taken from you. "You did not earn it; you cannot lose it. It is yours forever" (Elder Fale). He sees every part of us, and "knowing everything about you does not make Him love you less" (Sister Muñoz Spannaus). To anyone who fears they have wandered beyond the reach of God's love and covenant power: "I say to you, you have not" (Elder Morgan). By the power of the Atonement, "there is always a way back!" (Elder Rasband). "He has not forgotten you" (Elder Hathaway). And Elder Bednar, to faithful spouses whose marriages have broken: "No faithful disciple will ultimately be deprived of any eternal blessing God has promised because of another individual's unrighteous exercise of moral agency."
Promises of outward things (the windows of heaven opened, a family kept safe, a door opened) are fewer than ten of the 196. The rest are promises about the heart, and about who walks beside us. President Uchtdorf says it in a line: "we are not alone. We have the Savior, and we have each other." And through Him, as Elder Lebethoa promises, "today can be a new day and tomorrow can be a better day."

title: The conference opens and closes at a temple door
body: The first talk (Elder Gong) says temple 54 times; the other thirty-six talks say it 36 times combined, and twenty-three of them never say it. The last talk (President Oaks) announces that the Salt Lake Temple opens to the public on April 5, 2027, the first time since 1893. Elder Gong's own talk is a bookend too: it opens and closes on the same joke, 'Why did the temple workers cross the road?'

title: 531 scripture citations; Brother Reid's talk is the new crossroads
body: Each speaker leans on a home book: President Oaks's Sunday talk is 15 of 22 Book of Mormon, Bishop Douglas's 13 of 29 Doctrine and Covenants, Elder Renlund's 9 of 16 Old Testament (Israel in the wilderness), Elder Villanueva's 7 of 11 Old Testament (Malachi, Elijah). Elder Sinclair cites the most of anyone, 42, more than half of them New Testament; Elder Rasband is next with 40. Sixty-five passages are now shared by two or more talks. Brother Reid sits in sixteen of them, Elder Hathaway in ten. The most shared is Mosiah 18:8–11, the baptismal covenant to "mourn with those that mourn", in six talks; Alma 7:11–12, the Savior's succor, is in five. The closing hymn lists Doctrine and Covenants 76:41–42, inside the 76:39–43 Elder Gong cited in the first talk. And some talks stop one verse apart: Alma 34:32 (Elder Schmeil) and 34:33 (Elder Gong); Helaman 5:11 (Elder Hathaway) beside 5:12, which Elder Runia and Elder Rasband both cite.

title: The Sermon on the Mount, cited in both books
body: Two speakers set the Bible's Sermon on the Mount beside the Savior's sermon at the temple in Bountiful. President Christofferson cites Matthew 5:6 and 3 Nephi 12:6, and quotes the Book of Mormon wording: those who hunger and thirst after righteousness "shall be filled with the Holy Ghost." Bishop Douglas's footnote cites Matthew 5:48 and 3 Nephi 12:48 together, the call to be perfect: "Note the high love of the Savior, along with the high expectations."

title: Jairus's daughter, in Mark and in Luke, twice
body: Elder Hathaway and Elder Kearon, a session apart, both cite the raising of Jairus's daughter in two Gospels, Mark 5:35–42 and Luke 8:49–55. Elder Hathaway takes the Savior's words to the father, "Be not afraid, only believe," and echoes them to everyone still waiting. Elder Kearon takes the lifting, "He lifted the daughter of Jairus from the depths of death," and shows the painting Talitha Cumi, named for the words Jesus spoke to her.

title: Two Eyrings, the same two passages
body: Elder Matthew J. Eyring on Saturday and President Henry B. Eyring on Sunday both teach comfort, and both reach for the same two passages: Mosiah 18:8–9, the covenant to "mourn with those that mourn", and Alma 7:11–12, the Savior who knows how to succor His people. Both also look ahead: for Elder Eyring, "true sources of comfort will become more scarce"; for President Eyring, the Lord keeps His promise "today and in the hard days ahead".

title: The Good Samaritan four times, Bethesda three
body: Four talks cite the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30–37): President Farnes, Sister Chibota, President Uchtdorf and Elder Sinclair. Three of them, President Farnes, Sister Chibota and Elder Sinclair, also cite the pool of Bethesda (John 5). Both stories are about seeing someone others passed by. Sister Chibota builds her talk on the greeting sawubona, "I see you": "Where others saw labels, He saw beloved sons and daughters of God." Elder Sinclair's version is "quick to help and slow to judge".

title: Faith is the widest word; love is the loudest
body: Faith (135 mentions) is in 33 of the 37 talks and the closing hymn; only President Farnes, Elder Dunn, Elder Cook and Elder Sinclair never say it. Elder Andersen says it most, 25 times, in "Courage Born of Our Faith in Jesus Christ". Love is louder (263) but a little narrower, 32 talks: Elder Fale says it 34 times, Brother Reid 33, Elder Rasband 29, Elder Gilbert 28. Covenants (148, 26 talks) is carried by three speakers, Elder Morgan (24), Elder Schmeil (22) and Elder Bednar (20), while eleven talks never use it, among them both Elder Eyring and President Eyring. The closing hymn carries faith ("my one sure rock of faith") but never says covenant.

title: President Oaks is the voice other speakers build on
body: President Oaks is cited 46 times in 23 of the 35 talks he didn't give. Four talks are built on him: Elder Schmeil on 'Divine Helps for Mortality', Elder Gilbert on five principles from a devotional they gave together, President Christofferson, whose case against gambling runs on three Oaks lines, and Elder Kyungu, who takes up his April call to forgo contention: "This invitation ... comes from the living prophet." He is also a character in four stories. President Farnes's main story is Elder Oaks stopping him in a temple dressing room almost 20 years ago ("Brother, tell me how you are really doing") and, years later, not remembering it. Elder Dube remembers him having a "Trespassers will be prosecuted" sign taken off a mission gate in 1987. Sister Chibota quotes him calling her: "You've been called for who you are." Elder Andersen retells him accepting a hard call as a young lawyer: "Gathering all my faith, I accepted the call." His April 2026 talk "Alive in Christ" is cited in seven talks, and his February 2026 BYU devotional "Coming Closer to Jesus Christ" in four.

title: President Nelson is still cited almost as often as the living prophet
body: President Nelson is cited 29 times across 16 talks, against President Oaks's 46 across 23. Elder Gilbert (5) and Bishop Douglas (4) lean on him most; Bishop Douglas uses President Nelson's youth devotional to make the missionary call, so the call runs from one prophet to the next. President Oaks credits 'the covenant path' to President Nelson by name. Elder Giuffra quotes him on tithing: it "can break cycles of poverty in poor nations and families." On Sunday Elder Bednar takes his two words for a sealing from him, the "lateral" bond of husband and wife and the "vertical" bond to God, and Elder Dube his "Perfection Pending": "We come to Christ to be perfected."

title: Saturday morning runs on Joseph Smith
body: Each of the first six talks quotes or cites the Prophet Joseph Smith. Of the thirty-one talks after them, only four cite him: three on Saturday afternoon (Elder Renlund, Elder Chigbundu, Elder Morgan) and, on Sunday, Elder Bednar ("As the Lord revealed to the Prophet Joseph Smith"), and Bishop Douglas names him in passing: his closing scripture came "through Joseph Smith" to Thomas B. Marsh. Two of the six go to Liberty Jail: Sister Runia uses the Lord's answer to him there ("all these things shall give thee experience"), Elder Hathaway his cry ("O God, where art thou?"). Elder Morgan cites two lines Joseph Smith wrote there (Doctrine and Covenants 121:1 and 123:17) without naming the jail. Elder Sikahema quotes the First Vision, Elder Caussé and Elder Soares his teachings, Elder Gong his vision of the kingdoms of glory.

title: Grief runs through the conference
body: Three of the first five talks hold a death in the family. Sister Runia's oldest son, Ryan, died thirteen years ago; his seven-year-old son gave a Primary talk at the funeral about trusting the designer. Elder Sikahema's grandparents lost their infant son on an ocean voyage to hear an Apostle, then got back on the boat. Elder Hathaway tells of a missionary's father, Kelly, killed in an accident one week before she came home. In the afternoon Elder Eyring adds two more: a friend whose young married son died suddenly and could only say "I can't fix this," and a couple who lost a twin before birth, as he and his wife once did. On Sunday President Eyring's father, after his wife died, walked the hospital ward "to thank and to shake the hand of every nurse who had helped her." And Elder Stevenson's friend, a Buddhist temple priest in Japan grieving his wife, learns where her spirit is: "peace for despair, joy for sadness, hope for ashes."

title: Christ carries the load
body: Saturday afternoon keeps coming back to one point: Christ carries what we cannot. Elder Dunn's friend Ted quietly carried his pack for the last ten miles of a 100-mile race, and Christ is "an infinitely more amazing load-bearing Friend" who rescues "not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride." Elder Eyring starts from a grieving father's "I can't fix this." Elder Rasband ends on "He's got this!" Elder Dunn and Elder Eyring cite the same verse, Psalm 55:22: "Cast thy burden upon the Lord." On Sunday President Eyring adds Isaiah: the Savior has "borne [your] griefs, and carried [your] sorrows," and, with President Kimball, that God meets our needs "usually through another person".

title: For families with someone who has wandered
body: Elder Rasband lists what does not work with a loved one who has strayed: "We preach, cajole, argue, demand, lecture, ignore, sit them down to watch general conference, and even send them links to the talks, like this one." He says he and Sister Rasband have lived it, and asks: "never, never give up on those you love." Elder Morgan is the case from the other side: raised in another church, he finds his conversion came from his ancestors' covenants ("It was covenants"), which do not override a child's agency but leave "a discernible impact" on their posterity. Elder Fale: "you can always come home," pointing to Elder Gilbert's April talk "Come Home".

title: Tithes from Malachi, fasting from Isaiah
body: Elder Giuffra and Elder Soares, a session apart, teach the two offerings: tithing from Malachi's "windows of heaven", the fast from Isaiah 58. They meet in one person. Elder Giuffra's convert in Puerto Montt, Chile, who thought she could never pay, "arrived every week with her tithing envelope and... on the first Sunday of every month she also brought her fast offering." On Sunday Elder Villanueva takes his title from the same verse, "Prove me now herewith," and his evidence is small: a 20-liter propane tank that "had lasted far longer than she had expected," set beside Israel's clothes that were "not waxen old". His mother, separated and raising eight children, paid tithing the way the widow of Zarephath fed Elijah first.

title: "I Am a Child of God", three times
body: Elder Fale's talk is titled "I Am a Child of God" and ends on it: "I, Hutch 'Ungapapalangi Fale, am a child of God." The next day Sister Chibota's is titled "A Child of God" and asks us to "Replace worldly labels with these eternal truths: Child of God. Child of the covenant. Disciple of Jesus Christ." And Elder Stevenson tells of a small Primary boy who ran up to the stand at a devotional after an earthquake and sang the song.

title: Speak as peacemakers
body: Elder Kyungu takes up President Oaks's invitation to forgo contention and makes it concrete: fourteen phrases to give up, from "You are useless" to "I am tired of you", and twenty to use instead, from "Please" to "I don't want this to divide us"; "we too can bury the language of contention for peace." Elder Cook cites the same Oaks talk with President Nelson's "Peacemakers Needed". Elder Lebethoa settles his first argument as a newlywed with 3 Nephi 11: "he that hath the spirit of contention is not of me." President Uchtdorf: "If we are not one, we are not His."

title: The sacrament prayers, in five talks
body: Five talks cite the sacrament prayers: Doctrine and Covenants 20:77 in President Farnes, Elder Chigbundu, Elder Andersen and Sister Muñoz Spannaus, and Moroni 4:3 in President Farnes, Elder Andersen and President Uchtdorf. President Uchtdorf notices something new in them: "the sacrament is the only ordinance we receive during which we are not addressed by name."

title: Saturday afternoon teaches with everyday things
body: Cold oatmeal: Elder Renlund's heart-transplant survivor complains, "The oatmeal isn't hot, and the milk isn't cold!", and an asterisk that needs an eraser. The body's immunity (Elder Chigbundu). A glider riding air you cannot see (Elder Kearon). A friend named Ted at mile 90 (Elder Dunn). Baby pictures: "what had you done to earn our love?" (Elder Fale). Elder Rasband even gives the Savior everyday words: "In the vernacular, Jesus Christ says to all who grieve, 'I've got this!'"

title: Sixteen talks speak as 'I'
body: Sixteen of the 37 talks say 'I' more than 'we'. On Saturday: Sister Runia (61 to 56), Elder Caussé (58 to 24), Elder Sikahema (32 to 6), Bishop Douglas (20 to 8, and 'you' 43), President Farnes (78 to 54), Elder Giuffra (44 to 43), Elder Morgan (64 to 10) and Elder Dunn (56 to 38). On Sunday: Elder Fantone, Elder Dube, Sister Muñoz Spannaus (56 to 15), Elder Villanueva, Elder Sinclair, Elder Stevenson, Brother Reid and Elder Gilbert (46 to 36). Elder Kearon, Sister Chibota and Elder Andersen tell the most stories (8 each). Elder Gilbert's turning point is a failure of his own: 'I may have won the debate in the moment, but I lost the Spirit.'

title: Love and truth live in one talk
body: Of 48 truth words, 13 are Elder Gilbert's; his title says it: Teach Truth with Love. But love has spread: of 263 love words, Elder Fale has 34, Brother Reid 33 and Elder Rasband 29, ahead of Elder Gilbert's 28. Elder Fale's is a love you cannot lose: "You did not earn it; you cannot lose it." Brother Reid remembers his Primary teachers under a mango tree: "what I remember most is how they loved us." Elder Schmeil, Elder Sikahema, Elder Renlund, Elder Dunn and President Oaks in his closing remarks never say love at all.

title: Faith and secular learning, from two angles
body: President Oaks names two ways of knowing, the scientific and the spiritual, and says there is no ultimate conflict between them. Elder Gilbert tells of staying quiet while academic leaders attacked faith, and a chancellor later asking his help. Doubt and fading faith is the unspoken subject both share.

title: Some talks ask, some promise
body: Across the 37 talks there are 184 invitations and 196 promises. Elder Kearon asks the most (14), then Sister Muñoz Spannaus (12), with seven ways for young women to start, from "Protect your sleep" to "Limit cell phone use". Elder Soares and Elder Chigbundu promise the most (10 each); three of Elder Soares's answer his one invitation to live the fast in a higher and holier way. Bishop Douglas hangs all four of his promises on one invitation: serve a mission. Elder Sinclair asks seven times and promises once. Elder Sikahema makes no promise at all.

title: The shared picture is a path; the water runs deeper
body: Path pictures show up in 23 of the 37 talks (40 of them): a road, the covenant path, a detour, two paths (giving and taking), the trail to Zion. The closing hymn ends on one more: "the lonely road that leads to thine eternity". Water comes in 12 talks, and the first boat with it: Elder Sikahema's grandparents sail into a storm, bury their son, and get back on the boat. On Sunday it deepens: President Uchtdorf at his own baptism, "The pool is getting deeper and deeper, and I can't swim!", and Elder Sinclair's woman at the well, who "walked to the well that day as a pariah" and left with a purpose.

title: Phones, from gift to thief
body: Elder Sikahema holds up the cell phone as a gift: we can "easily see and hear His anointed servants", and so may take them for granted. Four talks later, President Christofferson holds it up as a danger: "tens of millions of [people] suddenly have casinos in their pockets." Same object, same morning, opposite warnings. On Sunday three more speakers take it up. Elder Andersen: "Our phone seems almost attached to our hand, bringing a flood of information, misinformation, and now artificial information." Elder Cook calls using the internet to bully "reprehensible", though "The Lord has inspired marvelous technology". Sister Muñoz Spannaus: "Limit cell phone use," because social media "is a thief of our peace of mind".

title: Instruments in His hands, echoes of His word
body: Elder Caussé and Elder Soares, three talks apart, make the same promise in the same words: you will "become instruments in His hands". Both also reach for an echo: for Elder Caussé, testimony and love echo each other; for Elder Soares, the latter-day fast is an echo of Isaiah.

title: Concrete announcements, with dates
body: 21 temples to be dedicated this year and 1 rededicated; the Salt Lake Temple open to the public April 5, 2027; a video series, Dedicate, starting right after the session. Bishop Douglas restates that a mission is a duty for young men and "a powerful, but optional, opportunity" for young women. And one forward-looking statement that reads as prophecy: records of Christ's visits to other nations, including the lost tribes, will come forth.

title: The conference ends where it began: a road and a veil
body: Elder Gong opened the conference with temple workers crossing the road "to help the people on the other side", and spoke of hearts softened "on both sides of the veil". The closing hymn's last two verses sing "the light beyond the veil of death" and "the lonely road that leads to thine eternity". Even the scripture listed under the hymn, Doctrine and Covenants 76:41–42, sits inside the passage Elder Gong cited.

title: The last word is a prophet's testimony
body: President Oaks closes his remarks with his witness that truth is found in the restored gospel. Then the congregation sings words written by an earlier prophet, President Gordon B. Hinckley: "I know that my Redeemer lives". The line is Job's (Job 19:25, listed under the hymn), so the conference closes on a testimony that runs from Job through a modern prophet to the people singing it.
